title: Hydrant and Booster Flow Testing, and Pump Testing
verdict: I would not sign this and I would not send a crew out on it. It is the best-drafted of the set — the citations I could check against primary sources all hold up exactly (WHS Reg 2011 (Qld) ss 48, 49, 51, 52, 56, 57, 58, 208(5)(b), 209, 210(1)(d), 213, 289(2)(e)/(3)(d), the six s 291 paragraphs quoted verbatim, ss 299-303; Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) ss 50, 53, 54, 55 including the 24-hour critical defect notice; the ESR 2013 citation has been correctly replaced with Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) and its Part 8 Division 3 is genuinely "Electrical work on or near energised electrical equipment"; AS 4602.1:2024 does exist and does supersede AS/NZS 4602.1:2011). Control ordering is correct in every step, no step claims a low residual, and steps[3] is honestly rated high. But it fails on the first test. steps[9].hazards[6] names "Unrestrained booster hose at pressure" and steps[9] then contains ten controls, not one of which restrains, straps or secures anything on the appliance delivery hose — the restraint controls in steps[7] and steps[8] are written for the crew's own hydrant test line, not for a brigade appliance pumping into the booster inlets at the highest pressure of the day. A crew reads that hazard, sees the step is dense with controls, and believes it is handled. Second: the whole diesel rescue architecture — steps[12].controls[9] and the emergency section's first numbered instruction — rests on stopping the engine from outside the room, while siteSpecificPrompts[8] openly admits there may be no external stop and steps[12].controls[0] never makes one a stop-work item. On a site with no remote stop, the standby person's procedure is to open a door and wait beside a running engine that is still filling the room with carbon monoxide around a person who is already down. Beyond those two: steps[5].controls[8] tells a technician to go back to the fire panel during a real fire in words the emergency section forbids; steps[10].controls[2] instructs lifting a lead off a float-charged start battery, which is an arc at the terminal of the hydrogen source steps[6].hazards[3] names, with no control and no eye protection; steps[8] never names that cracking the landing valve is what auto-starts both pumps; and the emergency section has no response for the snakes, spiders and wasps steps[4].hazards[3] names. Two level errors (steps[10].controls[4] / steps[11].controls[2] labelled engineering, steps[13].controls[1] labelled isolate) are minor but real. One further housekeeping point I have not listed as blocking: the hrcw array omits s 291(a), a risk of falling more than 2 m, which a deep below-ground booster chamber opened under steps[4] can present — the physical control is there in steps[4].controls[1], but the category should be on the tick-list. Fix the two fatal items and I would read it again expecting to sign.

blocking.field: steps[9].hazards[6] — "Unrestrained booster hose at pressure" — and the whole of steps[9].controls
blocking.problem: The step names "Unrestrained booster hose at pressure" as a hazard and then never controls it. All ten controls in steps[9] address other things: controls[0] bleeds stored energy before spanner work, controls[1] puts "barriers, or the vehicle positioned between the booster and any footpath or lane" — which protects the public, not the operator standing at the assembly — controls[2] is a test gauge and confirming the relief and non-return valves, controls[6] is "Stand to the side of a pressurised inlet", which addresses cap ejection, not a hose parting. The restraint controls that do exist, steps[7].controls[2] and steps[8].controls[4], are both written for the crew's own hydrant test line run off the landing valve ("every coupling on the line", "every coupling on the charged line"); neither reaches the appliance or test pump delivery hose feeding the booster inlets. That hose carries the highest pressure of the whole job — up to the recorded maximum boost pressure, which on a tall building is well above hydrant standing pressure — and the technician is standing at the assembly reading the gauge with it live beside them. With the step's worst named hazard uncontrolled, the "medium" residualRisk on steps[9] is also unsupported.
blocking.fix: Insert a new control as steps[9].controls[3], at engineering level, immediately after the existing controls[2] so it stays inside the engineering block and above the administrative block: "Hose restraints or safety straps fitted across every coupling on the appliance or test pump delivery hose and at each booster inlet connection before any pressure is raised, and checked again as the last thing before the operator is signalled up. These are the same restraints carried for the hydrant test line, and there are enough of them on the truck for the booster run as well. No restraints on that hose, no boost test — stop, raise it, come back with them. While pressure is being raised, everybody stands out of line with the hose run and clear of the inlets, not just to the side of them." Add "no hose restraints for the booster delivery hose" to the STOP-WORK LIST at steps[1].controls[0], which currently reads "no hose restraints on the truck" and should be explicit that the booster run needs its own.

blocking.field: steps[12].controls[0] and steps[12].controls[9], against siteSpecificPrompts[8] and the emergency section's "STANDBY PERSON - TECHNICIAN COLLAPSED INSIDE THE PUMP ROOM" item 1
blocking.problem: The rescue procedure for the single most likely way someone dies on this job depends on a control the document knows may not exist and never requires. Emergency item 1 says "Stop the engine from OUTSIDE - the external stop or the external isolator. Do not step into the room to reach a stop button." steps[12].controls[9] repeats it: the standby person "stop the engine from outside, open up, ring 000 and wait at the door." But siteSpecificPrompts[8] asks "Where is the external engine stop for the diesel, reachable from outside the room? If there is not one, the standby person needs to know that before the engine starts" — and then nothing follows. The stop-work list at steps[12].controls[0] is "no working mechanical ventilation, no standby person outside, no gas monitor in calibration, or a flue you cannot verify"; an external stop is not on it, nor on steps[1].controls[0], nor on steps[6].controls[2]. So a crew can lawfully, under this statement, run a diesel with no way to shut it down from outside. When the technician goes down, the standby person's entire procedure collapses to opening the door and waiting while the engine keeps running and keeps making carbon monoxide into the room the casualty is lying in. The "external isolator" named as the fallback will not help either: a running diesel is self-sustaining, and on a mechanically governed pumpset removing electrical supply or battery power does not necessarily stop it.
blocking.fix: Append to steps[12].controls[0], keeping it at eliminate level: "...and: no way to stop this engine from OUTSIDE the room. Before the engine turns over, the standby person is walked to the means of stopping it from outside — the remote or external stop button, or the fuel shut-off — and puts a hand on it. Where there is none, the diesel does not run today. Raise fitting a remote stop as a defect. Do not assume the electrical isolator will stop a running diesel; on most pumpsets it will not." Amend steps[12].controls[9] to read "...they stop the engine from outside using the stop they were shown at the pre-start, open up, ring 000 and wait at the door." Amend emergency item 1 to "Stop the engine from OUTSIDE, using the external stop or fuel shut-off you were shown before the engine started. Do not step into the room to reach a stop button." Change siteSpecificPrompts[8] from "If there is not one, the standby person needs to know that before the engine starts" to "If there is not one, the diesel does not run — see the stop-work list on the diesel run step."

blocking.field: steps[5].controls[8], against the "REAL ALARM OR REAL FIRE WHILE YOU ARE TESTING" paragraph of emergency
blocking.problem: One control instructs what another prohibits, and the dangerous version is the one sitting in the step a crew is reading at the time. steps[5].controls[8] is written as an absolute: "Standing instruction, no exceptions: on any real alarm, or any sign of a real fire, the impairment is lifted immediately - pumps to auto, isolation off, monitoring rung - and the arriving crew is told at the booster exactly what is isolated and what is back in service." The emergency section says the opposite for the case that matters: "If you are not at the panel, or it will take longer than seconds, leave it and go... Do not stay at a panel during a fire and do not go back to one." A technician who is at the booster or in the pump room when the building goes up, reading the step he is working to, is being told by "no exceptions" and "immediately" to go back through a building on fire to a fire indicator panel.
blocking.fix: Replace steps[5].controls[8] with, at the same administrative level and in the same slot: "Standing instruction on any real alarm or any sign of a real fire. If you are AT the panel and it takes seconds — pumps to auto, isolation off, then go. If you are not at the panel, or anything at all is between you and it, LEAVE IT AND GO. You do not go back to a panel during a fire and you do not stay at one. Either way, get to the warden and to the arriving fire crew at the assembly area or the booster and tell them plainly what is isolated, what state both pumps are in, which zones are affected and where the fire watch is. Ring the monitoring company from outside, once you are clear. Getting that information to the brigade matters more than the state of the panel. See the emergency section of this statement."

blocking.field: steps[10].controls[2] ("or the battery leads lifted") and steps[10].controls[7], against steps[6].hazards[3] and steps[12].hazards[5]
blocking.problem: The statement names hydrogen gassing at the start batteries twice — steps[6].hazards[3] "Battery gassing hydrogen, acid on the terminals" and steps[12].hazards[5] "Diesel and oil, and hydrogen off gassing batteries" — and controls the ignition sources it happened to think of, at steps[6].controls[8]: "No smoking, no naked flame, no grinder in this room." It then instructs the crew, at steps[10].controls[2], to create an ignition source at the exact point of maximum hydrogen concentration: "both start battery banks isolated, or the battery leads lifted, with your padlock and danger tag on the battery isolators." Breaking a lead on a battery arcs at the terminal, with the technician's face directly over it. Fire pump start batteries sit on a permanent charger — steps[6].controls[8] has the crew confirm "the charger is on float" — so they are gassing every time anyone touches them. There is no control for this anywhere in steps[10], and steps[10].controls[7] is the only PPE in the step: "Sleeves down, no loose clothing, no lanyard, no rings or watch anywhere near a pumpset. Hearing protection to hand." No eye protection, no gloves, for work at a battery that can burst and spray electrolyte.
blocking.fix: Amend steps[10].controls[2], keeping it at isolate level and in its slot, so the battery clause reads: "...AND both start battery banks isolated. Use the battery isolator switch where there is one — do not lift leads if a switch will do it. Where a lead must be lifted: turn the battery charger OFF first and leave the room's ventilation running, break the earth/negative lead first and refit it last, keep your face and body out of line with the top of the battery, and use an insulated spanner so the tool cannot bridge a terminal to the frame. A start battery on float charge is giving off hydrogen at the terminals, and an arc there is the ignition source this statement names at the pre-start. Fit your padlock and danger tag to the battery isolator, or to the lifted lead where there is no isolator..." Amend steps[10].controls[7] to: "Sleeves down, no loose clothing, no lanyard, no rings or watch anywhere near a pumpset. Goggles or a face shield and gloves for any work at the start batteries — electrolyte, and a case that can split. Hearing protection to hand."

blocking.field: emergency — the section as a whole, against steps[4].hazards[3]
blocking.problem: steps[4].hazards[3] names "Snakes, spiders, wasps and vermin in a pit that has been shut for twelve months" and steps[4] controls it sensibly for prevention (controls[4] torch and tap before a hand goes in, controls[7] gloves and boots). But the emergency section, which is the part a crew actually opens when something has happened, has an entry for gas exposure, a technician down in the pump room, a burst hose, high pressure water injection, electric shock, flooding, being struck by a vehicle, a real fire, and notifiable incident reporting — and nothing at all for a bite or a sting. In Queensland an in-ground hydrant or valve pit that has been shut since the last annual is precisely where an eastern brown shelters, and the ways people die of that bite are the wrong first aid: washing the site, applying a tourniquet, or walking the casualty to the vehicle. Training lists HLTAID011, but every other hazard on this job got its own written response and this one did not.
blocking.fix: Add a paragraph to emergency, immediately after the "WATER JET OR HIGH PRESSURE INJECTION INJURY" paragraph: "SNAKE BITE, OR ANY BITE OR STING WITH A REACTION: keep them still and lie them down where they are. Do not walk them to the vehicle, do not wash the bite, do not cut it, do not suck it and do not use a tourniquet. Pressure immobilisation bandage: a broad firm bandage straight over the bite, then bandage the whole limb from the fingers or toes upward, as firm as for a badly sprained ankle, and splint the limb so it cannot move. Mark the bite site on the OUTSIDE of the bandage. Ring 000, say snake bite, give the address and say exactly how to reach you. Stay with them, watch their breathing and be ready to start CPR. For a bee or wasp sting where the face or throat swells, they wheeze, or they collapse, treat it as anaphylaxis: adrenaline autoinjector if there is one on site, lie them flat, ring 000. Every bite goes to hospital even if they say they feel fine." Add to siteSpecificPrompts: "Is there an adrenaline autoinjector on site or on the truck, and does anyone on the crew carry one? Where is the nearest hospital and how long to it?"

blocking.problem: A hazard of this work that the step never names at all. steps[8] is "Charge the line and flow the hydrant at full bore", and cracking the landing valve at full bore is exactly what drops system pressure and auto-starts the electric pump, and then the diesel behind it. The nine hazards listed cover hose whip, reaction force, the jet, water hammer, flooding, wet ground, legionella, tank level and discharge water — nothing about the pumps starting. There is no control saying who may be in the pump room while the flow is running, and on a pumped system a two-person crew routinely has one person in there catching the pump running pressures for the Form 72. That person gets a diesel starting beside them with no warning, no start-up delay, and possibly no hearing protection in and no gas monitor on, because the pump-room PPE controls all live in steps[6] and steps[12] and this is neither. The control that would cover it, steps[10].controls[6] ("treat both as able to start at any moment"), sits two steps further down the document and is written about the period between tests, not about the hydrant flow.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[8].hazards: "Opening the landing valve drops system pressure and auto-starts the electric pump, and then the diesel behind it, with no warning and nobody at the controls." Add a control to steps[8] at administrative level as the new first entry of the administrative block, immediately before the existing controls[6] ("Open the landing valve slowly"): "Before the landing valve is cracked, say out loud that this flow will start both pumps on the pressure drop, and confirm where every person on site is. If nobody needs to be in the pump room during the flow, nobody is in it. Anybody who does have to be in there for the running readings has hearing protection in and the gas monitor on their collar BEFORE the valve is opened, stands clear of the couplings, shafts and fans, and knows the diesel can start behind them at any moment — the pumps are in auto and there is no warning and no start-up delay."

blocking.problem: Both read "Do the mains failure test by turning the external isolator handle only. Never pull a fuse, lift a cover or open a door to make the pump fail." That is a method instruction plus a prohibition, which is administrative. Nothing in it is a physical change to the plant. Because it carries the engineering label, in both steps it is ranked above every administrative control below it — including steps[10].controls[5], the "DUTY AND STANDBY" control which is the one that actually keeps a person off the diesel coupling when the mains failure test starts it. A crew reading down and doing the first thing they can do is being handed a ranking that puts a prohibition above the warning that matters.
blocking.fix: Change steps[10].controls[4] and steps[11].controls[2] to "level": "administrative". In steps[10], move it to become the first entry of the administrative block, i.e. immediately before the "DUTY AND STANDBY" control, so the array runs eliminate, isolate, isolate, isolate, administrative (mains failure method), administrative (duty and standby), administrative (between tests), ppe. In steps[11], move it to become the first entry of the administrative block, immediately before "Call 'STARTING THE PUMP' out loud", leaving controls[3] ("Coupling and fan guards on and bolted") as the only engineering control in that step — which is correct, since a bolted guard is a physical barrier.

blocking.problem: The control reads "Let the engine, the manifold, the flue and the cooling system cool before covers, caps, hoses or anything near them is touched. Thirty minutes minimum, longer on a hot day. Nothing about a hot cooling system looks hot." That is a wait-and-do-not-touch rule that a tired person at the end of a job has to keep in their head — administrative, not isolation. Isolation means something physically between the person and the hazard. Labelled isolate, it outranks steps[13].controls[2], which is the step's only genuine engineering control.
blocking.fix: Change steps[13].controls[1] to "level": "administrative" and move it to the head of the administrative block, immediately after controls[2] ("Close the pump room fire door...") and before "Close the landing valve slowly". If a real isolate-level control is wanted in the slot it vacates, add one that earns the label: "level": "isolate", "control": "Where a hot manifold, flue or cooling pipe is within reach of where the pack-up work happens, put something physical in front of it — a barrier, a cone-and-tape stand, or shut the room and keep everyone out — until it has cooled. Do not rely on people remembering which parts are hot."

blocking.field: emergency — the section as a whole, against steps[8].hazards[6] and steps[8].controls[9]
blocking.problem: steps[8].hazards[6] names "Aerosol off a main that has held stagnant water for twelve months - legionella in the breathing zone", and steps[8].controls[9] handles it honestly at the time — stand upwind, keep the plume out of the breathing zone, reposition rather than wear it. What is missing is the other half: legionellosis presents two to ten days later as an ordinary flu, and a technician who does not connect it to a hydrant flow will be sent home with a viral diagnosis. There is no respiratory protection anywhere in the ppe array either, which is a defensible call for outdoor work upwind, but it makes the delayed-symptom instruction the only remaining safeguard and it is not written down anywhere.
blocking.fix: Add a short paragraph to emergency, after the "WATER JET OR HIGH PRESSURE INJECTION INJURY" paragraph: "FLU SYMPTOMS IN THE WEEK AFTER A FLOW TEST: anybody who comes down with fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, a cough or shortness of breath in the two to ten days after flowing a hydrant sees a doctor and TELLS THEM they were in the spray from a fire main that had been standing for twelve months. Say the word legionella. It is treatable and it is missed when nobody mentions the exposure. Tell the Safe QLD supervisor as well — a confirmed case is notifiable." Add a line to steps[8].controls[9] after "Do not just wear it and get on with it": "And if you get flu symptoms in the week after, see the emergency section — it matters that the doctor is told about this exposure."
